name: Quitting smoking / vaping

lead: Smokers show a characteristic aged look: wrinkles and grey, sallow skin. Some people quit hoping to look younger.
Observational data show the features are less common in former smokers, but reversal is not well established.

paras: Smoking raises collagen-degrading enzymes, narrows blood vessels and increases oxidative stress.
Smoking carries major documented harms including cancers, heart and lung disease. Quitting is associated with falling lung cancer risk over years.

lead: Quitting smoking or vaping is a practice appearance communities cite for reducing premature skin aging. Smoker's face describes facial changes seen in smokers, including a characteristic wrinkle pattern and sallow grey skin tone.[1]

A 1985 BMJ study by D. Model reported certain facial features in about 46% of continuing smokers and 8% of former smokers who had smoked for a decade.[1] Proposed mechanisms include raised matrix metalloproteinases degrading collagen and elastin, vasoconstriction and oxidative stress.[1] The sources reviewed do not address vaping and skin.

paras: Smoking is classed as an extrinsic aging factor. It lowers oxygen delivery to skin, depletes antioxidants such as vitamin C and impairs enzymes that clear matrix debris, leaving skin thinner and sagging.[1] Smoking is also linked to hair loss, gum disease and tooth staining.[1]

Lung cancer risk begins falling soon after quitting and drops about 50% after 10 years; about 70% of smokers intend to quit, while 3 to 5% succeed.[2] Whether facial changes reverse after quitting is not addressed in the sources reviewed, which report only that the features were far less common in former smokers.[1]
Quitting is mentioned in skin-aging and health routines. No appearance outcome data on vaping cessation were found.
No studies found on quitting vaping for appearance. For smoking, one observational study compared facial features of current, former and non-smokers.[1]

timeline.event: Model publishes 'Smoker's face: an underrated clinical sign?' in the BMJ.[1]
